def-eiv-classical.title: Classical measurement error
def-eiv-classical.html: Suppose x is observed only through w=x+u. The error u is classical if E(u)=0, Cov(u)=Σuu, and u is independent of (x,z,ε).

def-eiv-instrument.title: Instruments
def-eiv-instrument.html:
A random q-vector z is a vector of instruments for @eq-eiv-structural-equation, with random regressor p-vector x, if

  1. exogeneity: E(ze)=0;

  2. relevance: Σzx=E(zx⊤) has rank p, which requires q≥p;

and Σzz=E(zz⊤) is positive definite.

def-eiv-reliability.title: Reliability ratio
def-eiv-reliability.html: The reliability ratio of W=X+U is λ=σx2σx2+σu2=Var(X)Var(W). If z is measured exactly, let 𝛔𝛔σx⋅z2=σx2−σzx⊤Σzz−1σzx be the residual variance of X after its best linear prediction from z (@thm-proj-blp), where 𝛔σzx=Cov(z,X). The reliability given z is λx∣z=σx⋅z2σx⋅z2+σu2.

eq-eiv-2sls.html: 𝛃β^2SLS=(X⊤MZX)−1X⊤MZy.

eq-eiv-composite.html: Y=α+βW+(ε−βU).

eq-eiv-corrected.html: 𝛉A^n=1n∑i=1n(sisi⊤−Di),θ^mm=A^n−11n∑i=1nsiyi.

eq-eiv-deming.html: βδ=σyy−δσww+(σyy−δσww)2+4δσwy22σwy,

eq-eiv-normal-structural.html: (σwwσwyσwyσyy)=(σx2+σu2βσx2βσx2β2σx2+σ2).

eq-eiv-simex-limit.html: 𝛃𝛑gx(ζ)=βxσx⋅z2σx⋅z2+(1+ζ)σu2,gz(ζ)=βz+(1+ζ)σu2σx⋅z2+(1+ζ)σu2βxπ,

eq-eiv-structural-equation.html: 𝛃yi=x(i)⊤β+ei,E(x(i)ei)≠0,

eq-eiv-true-model.html: 𝛃𝛃Y=α+βx⊤x+βz⊤z+ε,

eq-eiv-weak-representation.html: σeσv⋅ρη+1−ρ2ξμ+η,η,ξ∼iidN(0,1).

exm-eiv-attenuation.title: One reading instead of long-run pressure
exm-eiv-attenuation.title_html: One reading instead of long-run pressure
exm-eiv-attenuation.html: In the running example, regressing y on the true x gives slope 0.0755 (standard error 0.0050). Regressing on the first clinic reading gives 0.0499 (standard error 0.0046), a ratio of 0.661, close to λ=0.64; the limit is λβ=0.0512. The usual 95% interval, [0.0409,0.0589], misses 0.08, and in 4000 repeated samples the observed coverage was 0.000. The standard error measures variability around λβ, not the distance from λβ to β. The residual variance tends to 1+0.64⋅0.082⋅81=1.3318 by @thm-eiv-attenuation(d).

exm-eiv-berkson.title: Concentrations set on a dial
exm-eiv-berkson.html: Five solutions are prepared at each nominal concentration 10,20,…,60 mg/L (n=30); the achieved concentration adds N(0,42) error, and the response is 2+0.5x+ε, ε∼N(0,32). Regressing on the nominal concentrations in 20000 simulated experiments gives a mean slope of 0.4994 and a mean s2 of 13.01, matching σ2+β2σu2=9+0.25⋅16=13. The nominal 95% t intervals for the slope covered 0.5 in a proportion 0.952 of the experiments.

exm-eiv-calibration.title: Calibrating the mean reading
exm-eiv-calibration.html: The replicates estimate the error variance of the mean reading as 37.04. The calibrated pressure x^i has standard deviation 10.36, against 13.11 for the mean reading: each reading is shrunk towards what age predicts. Regressing y on (1,x^,age) gives 0.0757 and 0.0018, exactly the moment correction of @exm-eiv-replicates, by @prp-eiv-calibration(d).

exm-eiv-identified-set.title: The interval for the blood-pressure study
exm-eiv-identified-set.title_html: The interval for the blood-pressure study
exm-eiv-identified-set.html: For the first reading in the running example, the sample covariances are sww=216.21, swy=10.786 and syy=1.889. The compatible slopes form the interval [0.0499,0.1752], and the squared correlation is 0.285. It contains the true 0.08, whose implied variances σx2=134.8, σu2=81.4 and σ2=1.026 are close to the generating 144, 81 and 1, but the data cannot prefer them to those of any other slope in the interval (Figure 24.2.1).

exm-eiv-leak.title: Age looks important
exm-eiv-leak.html: Add age to the regression on the first reading. Theory predicts a coefficient of λx∣zβ=0.0457 for the reading and (1−0.571)⋅0.08⋅0.6=0.0206 per year for age, which truly has no effect. The sample gives 0.0455 for the reading and 0.0182 for age, with standard error 0.0070 and p-value 0.0098. In 4000 repeated samples the t test of “no age effect” rejected at the 5% level in a proportion 0.812 of them. Figure 24.1.1(b) shows both limits as functions of the reliability.

exm-eiv-method-comparison.title: Comparing two assays
exm-eiv-method-comparison.html:
Sixty specimens with true concentrations uniform on [2,20] are measured by method A with error standard deviation 0.8 and by method B, which reads 0.3+1.05x with error standard deviation 1.0, so δ=1.5625. The four slopes are

Method Slope
least squares of B on A 1.0042
Deming, δ=1.5625 1.0308
orthogonal (δ=1, unjustified) 1.0382
least squares of A on B, inverted 1.0709

with Deming intercept 0.482. Over 20000 simulated studies the mean slopes were 1.0262 for least squares, attenuated by 27/(27+0.64)=0.9768, and 1.0505 for Deming. With B in units ten times smaller, orthogonal regression gives 1.0703 (converted back to the original units) instead of 1.0382.

exm-eiv-replicates.title: Correcting with two readings
exm-eiv-replicates.html: In the running example, regress y on (1,w¯,age), where w¯ is the mean of the two readings. The reliability of the mean is 144/(144+40.5)=0.780, and given age it is 108/(108+40.5)=0.727. The naive coefficients are 0.0562 (standard error 0.0054) for blood pressure and 0.0120 (standard error 0.0070) for age. The replicates estimate σu2 as 74.1 (true 81), and @eq-eiv-corrected gives β~x=0.0757 (0.0076),β~age=0.0018 (0.0076), with sandwich standard errors. The 95% interval for βx is [0.0608,0.0905], and the spurious age effect is gone. The standard error is 1.40 times the naive one: the bias is paid for in variance. With σu2=81 known the estimate would be 0.0782. In 10000 repeated samples the corrected intervals covered 0.08 in a proportion 0.949, the naive ones in 0.013.

exm-eiv-second-reading.title: The second reading as an instrument
exm-eiv-second-reading.title_html: The second reading as an instrument
exm-eiv-second-reading.html: Instrument the first reading with the second, and let age and the constant instrument themselves. The IV estimates are 0.0708 for blood pressure, with standard error 0.0085 (0.0081 from the sandwich), and 0.0054 for age (standard error 0.0081). The spurious age effect has gone. The first-stage F statistic for the second reading is 160.1, a strong instrument. The correct residuals give σ^e2=1.438, estimating σ2+β2σu2=1.5184; the second-stage residuals give 1.376. The moment correction of @exm-eiv-replicates gave 0.0757 with standard error 0.0076. It uses both readings symmetrically, while IV uses one only as an instrument and pays in precision. But IV needs no estimate of the error variance, and the instrument need only be correlated with X, not a second unbiased reading of it.

exm-eiv-simex.title: SIMEX for the blood-pressure study
exm-eiv-simex.html:
Apply SIMEX to the regression on the mean reading and age, with error variance 37.04, grid {0,0.5,1,1.5,2} and B=200 (Figure 24.5.1). Extrapolating to ζ=−1:

Coefficient naive SIMEX, quadratic SIMEX, a+b/(c+ζ) moment correction truth
blood pressure 0.0562 0.0709 0.0744 0.0757 0.08
age 0.0120 0.0042 0.0024 0.0018 0

The rational extrapolant nearly reproduces the moment correction; the quadratic stops short, and by @prp-eiv-simex(c) its large-sample limit is 0.0749, only 0.77 of the way from the naive limit 0.0582 to 0.08, and 0.0030 for age. A pairs bootstrap (@def-bs-bootstrap) over patients, re-estimating the error variance and rerunning SIMEX (B=50, 200 resamples), gives standard error 0.0076 for the rational SIMEX slope, as for the moment correction.

exm-eiv-weak.title: How weak is too weak?
exm-eiv-weak.html:
With n=200, β=1, σe=σv=1 and ρ=0.9, least squares tends to about 1.9 for a weak instrument. In 20000 samples for each concentration:

μ2 median quartiles coverage of nominal 95% Wald interval
1 1.298 0.711 to 1.646 0.843
10 1.008 0.740 to 1.181 0.921
100 1.002 0.929 to 1.064 0.947

With μ2=1 the median moves a third of the way to the least squares limit, a proportion 0.200 of estimates fall outside [−1,3], and the Wald interval undercovers, as it still does at μ2=10 (Figure 24.4.1).

exr-eiv-2sls-optimal.title: C2
exr-eiv-2sls-optimal.html: Let F be a fixed q×p matrix with Σzx⊤F nonsingular, and consider the IV estimator with instruments ZF. Under homoscedasticity its asymptotic covariance is σe2(F⊤Σzx)−1F⊤ΣzzF(Σzx⊤F)−1. Show that this is never smaller, in the nonnegative definite ordering, than σe2H−1, with equality when F=Σzz−1Σzx, which is the population version of 2SLS.

exr-eiv-anderson-rubin.title: C1
exr-eiv-anderson-rubin.html: In @eq-eiv-structural-equation with x=(1,W), let z=(1,z1) with z1 a k-vector of excluded instruments, and suppose e is independent of z and N(0,σe2). To test H0:β=β0, regress y−β0w on z and compute the F statistic for z1. Show that under H0 it has an exact F(k,n−k−1) distribution, whatever the strength of the instruments. This is the test of Anderson and Rubin (1949). Inverting it gives a confidence set for β. Show that for k=1 the set is of the form in @prp-ci-fieller.

exr-eiv-berkson-quadratic.title: B1
exr-eiv-berkson-quadratic.html: Let Y=β0+β1X+β2X2+β3X3+ε and X=W+U with Berkson error U∼N(0,σu2) independent of W and ε. Compute E(Y∣W). Which coefficients of a cubic regression on W are biased, and by how much? What happens for a quadratic?

exr-eiv-bound.title: A2
exr-eiv-bound.html: In @prp-eiv-nonidentified, suppose it is known only that the reliability is at least λ0∈(0,1]. Show that the compatible slopes are those between b1 and min(|b2|,|b1|/λ0) in magnitude, with the sign of b1. Evaluate the interval for @exm-eiv-identified-set with λ0=0.5.

exr-eiv-classify.title: A1
exr-eiv-classify.html: Classify each regressor error as classical, Berkson or neither, and say whether it biases the slope: (a) weight from a noisy scale; (b) a prescribed dose, when patients take a random fraction of it with mean one; (c) income rounded down to the nearest 10,000.

exr-eiv-conditional-reliability.title: B1
exr-eiv-conditional-reliability.html: For a scalar X and a scalar exactly measured Z, show that λx∣z=λ−ρwz21−ρwz2, where ρwz is the correlation between W and Z. Check the formula on the running example, and deduce that λx∣z<λ whenever ρwz≠0 and λ<1.

exr-eiv-correlated-replicates.title: A2
exr-eiv-correlated-replicates.html: If the errors of two readings are correlated, Cov(U1,U2)=κ, find the limit of the IV slope in simple regression that instruments W1 with W2. In which direction is it biased when κ>0?

exr-eiv-functional-ml.title: C1
exr-eiv-functional-ml.html:
In the functional model wi=xi+ui, yi=α+βxi+εi, with ui,εi independent N(0,σ2) (equal, unknown variances) and x1,…,xn unknown constants:

  1. show that, for fixed (α,β), maximizing the likelihood over each xi leaves di2=(yi−α−βwi)2/(1+β2), the squared perpendicular distance from (wi,yi) to the line;

  2. deduce that the maximum likelihood line is the orthogonal regression line of Section 24.3, and that σ^ML2=(2n)−1∑id^i2;

  3. show that σ^ML2→σ2/2 in probability, assuming the line is estimated consistently. Compare @exm-opt-neyman-scott.

exr-eiv-iv-simple.title: A1
exr-eiv-iv-simple.html: For x=(1,W) and z=(1,Z), show that the IV slope is szy/szw, the ratio of two sample covariances. Show that the population ratio equals β when Z is correlated with X and uncorrelated with U and ε.

exr-eiv-no-mean.title: C1
exr-eiv-no-mean.html: In the normal structural model with known σu2 and n≥3, show that β~=swy/(sww−σu2) has E|β~|=∞. (Condition on W1,…,Wn, and use the fact that sww has a continuous density that is positive at σu2.)

exr-eiv-normal-variance.title: B2
exr-eiv-normal-variance.html: In simple regression with centred variables and known σu2, take D=diag(0,σu2) in @thm-eiv-correction and suppose (X,U,ε) are jointly normal and independent. Show that the asymptotic variance of n(β~−β) is σw2σv2+β2σu4σx4,σv2=σ2+β2σu2. Compare it with σ2/σx2, the asymptotic variance when X is observed. What does this give for the running example with the mean of two readings?

exr-eiv-r2.title: B2
exr-eiv-r2.html: In the setting of @thm-eiv-attenuation(b), show that the population R2 of Y on W equals λ times the population R2 of Y on X. Measurement error lowers the apparent strength of a relation twice: once through the slope and once through the residual variance.

exr-eiv-rc-simple.title: A1
exr-eiv-rc-simple.html: In simple regression without z, show directly that regression calibration (@prp-eiv-calibration) with the linear calibration x^=w¯+λ^(w−w¯), λ^=(sww−σu2)/sww, gives the slope β^/λ^, where β^ is the naive slope.

exr-eiv-reliability-correlation.title: A1
exr-eiv-reliability-correlation.html: Show that λ=Corr(W,X)2. If W1=X+U1 and W2=X+U2 are two readings with independent classical errors of the same variance, show that Corr(W1,W2)=λ. This is why test–retest correlations are used as reliability estimates.

exr-eiv-replicate-D.title: A2
exr-eiv-replicate-D.html: Show that the matrix Di defined from m replicates has expectation Σuu/m, the covariance matrix of u¯i, padded with zeros.

exr-eiv-reverse-limit.title: B2
exr-eiv-reverse-limit.html: In the normal structural model, show that the reciprocal of the least squares slope of W on Y converges to b2=β+σ2/(βσx2), so that it overstates |β| exactly when there is equation error. Evaluate b2 for the population of the running example and compare it with @exm-eiv-identified-set.

exr-eiv-rounding.title: C1
exr-eiv-rounding.html: Regressors are often recorded after rounding. Model this as S=T+Δ with T the true model matrix and Δ a fixed matrix of rounding errors, and suppose 𝛉E(Y)=Tθ, Cov(Y)=σ2I. Use @prp-lm-misspecified to show that least squares on S has bias 𝛉−(S⊤S)−1S⊤Δθ, that its covariance matrix is exactly σ2(S⊤S)−1, and that the expected residual mean square is at least σ2.

exr-eiv-sign-reversal.title: B3
exr-eiv-sign-reversal.html: Let t=(X1,X2) have unit variances and correlation ρ, let X1 be measured exactly and X2 with classical error of variance σu2, and let 𝛉θ=(β1,β2). Show that the limit of the coefficient of X1 is β1+(1−λ2∣1)ρβ2, where λ2∣1=(1−ρ2)/(1−ρ2+σu2). With ρ=0.5, σu2=1, β2=1 and β1=−0.2, show that the sign of the first coefficient is reversed.

exr-eiv-simex-logistic.title: C1
exr-eiv-simex-logistic.html: Simulate a logistic regression Pr(Y=1∣X)=1/(1+e−(α+βX)) with X∼N(0,1), β=1, n=2000, and a reading W=X+U with σu2=0.5. Compare the naive estimate, regression calibration (@prp-eiv-calibration: replace W by E(X∣W)), and SIMEX with quadratic and rational extrapolants, over repeated samples. Which is closest to β?

exr-eiv-simex-quadratic.title: B1
exr-eiv-simex-quadratic.html: In simple regression with reliability λ, write g(ζ)=λβ/{1+ζ(1−λ)}. Show that the quadratic through (ζ,g(ζ)) for ζ=0,1,2 takes the value 3g(0)−3g(1)+g(2) at ζ=−1. Evaluate it for λ=0.5 and λ=0.64, as fractions of β.

exr-eiv-spearman.title: A1
exr-eiv-spearman.html: Prove Spearman’s correction: if Wk=Xk+Uk for k=1,2, with classical errors independent of each other and of (X1,X2), then Corr(W1,W2)=λ1λ2Corr(X1,X2).

exr-eiv-spearman-brown.title: B1
exr-eiv-spearman-brown.html: Let W¯ be the mean of m readings with independent classical errors of variance σu2, and let λ be the reliability of one reading. Show that the reliability of W¯ is λm=mλ1+(m−1)λ. How many readings are needed in the running example for the attenuation factor to reach 0.9?

exr-eiv-validation.title: B2
exr-eiv-validation.html: A validation subsample of nv patients has the true x measured along with (w,z), and the main sample has only (w,z,y). Describe regression calibration using the validation data. Which of the assumptions of @prp-eiv-calibration does it need, and which does it avoid? Why does using the validation patients’ x directly in the outcome regression not help if their y is not recorded?

exr-eiv-wald-grouping.title: B1
exr-eiv-wald-grouping.html: Let gi∈{0,1} be a group indicator, and let z(i)=(1,gi) instrument x(i)=(1,wi). Show that the IV slope is (y¯1−y¯0)/(w¯1−w¯0), the difference of group means of y divided by that of w. This is Wald’s (1940) estimator. Show that it is consistent if g is independent of (U,ε) and E(X∣g) differs between the groups. Explain why forming the groups by splitting at the median of w itself, as Wald proposed, does not satisfy these conditions under classical error.

lem-eiv-2sls.title: Two-stage least squares as projection
lem-eiv-2sls.html:
Let Z have full column rank and X⊤MZX be nonsingular, and let X^=MZX be the matrix of first-stage fitted values, obtained by regressing each column of X on Z.

  1. 𝛃β^2SLS is the least squares coefficient of y on X^, and also the IV estimator with instruments X^: 𝛃β^2SLS=(X^⊤X^)−1X^⊤y=(X^⊤X)−1X^⊤y.

  2. Columns of X that are also columns of Z are unchanged by the first stage.

  3. If q=p and Z⊤X is nonsingular, 𝛃𝛃β^2SLS=β^IV.

prp-eiv-berkson.title: Berkson error in linear regression
prp-eiv-berkson.html: Let 𝛃Y=α+β⊤x+ε and x=w+u, where w is fixed or random and, given w, the errors u and ε are independent, with means zero, covariance matrix Σuu and variance σ2, not depending on w. Then, given w, 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(Y∣w)=α+β⊤w,Var(Y∣w)=σ2+β⊤Σuuβ, and if u and ε are normal, so is Y given w. Independent observations of this kind therefore satisfy the linear model in the recorded w, with the same coefficients and error variance 𝛃𝛃σ2+β⊤Σuuβ.

prp-eiv-calibration.title: Regression calibration
prp-eiv-calibration.html:
Suppose 𝛃𝛃E(Y∣x,z)=α+βx⊤x+βz⊤z and the error is nondifferential, and let m(w,z)=E(x∣w,z).

  1. 𝛃𝛃E(Y∣w,z)=α+βx⊤m(w,z)+βz⊤z.

  2. If moreover Var(Y∣x,z)=σ2 and Cov(x∣w,z)=C does not depend on (w,z), as when (x,z,u) is jointly normal, then 𝛃𝛃Var(Y∣w,z)=σ2+βx⊤Cβx. The regression of Y on (1,m(w,z),z) is then a homoscedastic linear model with the original coefficients.

  3. Without distributional assumptions, let the error be classical with finite second moments. With t=(1,x⊤,z⊤)⊤, s=(1,w⊤,z⊤)⊤, A=E(tt⊤) positive definite and S=E(ss⊤), the best linear predictor of t from s is t^=AS−1s, and the best linear predictor of Y from t^ is 𝛉θ⊤t^, where 𝛉𝛃𝛃θ=(α,βx⊤,βz⊤)⊤.

  4. The sample version of (c) reproduces the method-of-moments estimator exactly. If S^=n−1∑isisi⊤, A^=S^−D for a symmetric matrix D with A^ nonsingular, and t^i=A^S^−1si, then the least squares coefficients of y on the t^i are A^−1n−1∑isiyi, which is @eq-eiv-corrected with Di=D.

prp-eiv-deming.title: Deming regression
prp-eiv-deming.html:
Let (W,Y) have covariances σww,σwy,σyy with σwy≠0 and σwwσyy≥σwy2, and let δ>0 be known.

  1. The equations σww=σx2+σu2, σwy=βσx2, σyy=β2σx2+δσu2 have exactly one solution with σx2>0, namely βδ=σyy−δσww+(σyy−δσww)2+4δσwy22σwy,{#eq-eiv-deming}

    and for it σu2≥0. The slope βδ lies in the interval of @prp-eiv-nonidentified. It tends to b2 as δ→0 and to b1 as δ→∞.

  2. For δ=1, β1 is the slope of the line that minimizes the mean squared perpendicular distance from (W,Y), whose direction is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix of (W,Y) for its largest eigenvalue. For general δ, βδ is δ times the δ=1 slope computed for (W,Y/δ).

prp-eiv-functional.title: Attenuation with fixed true values
prp-eiv-functional.html: Let t1,t2,⋯∈Rp be fixed vectors with first coordinate 1, such that n−1∑i=1ntiti⊤→A, a positive definite matrix. Let 𝛉yi=ti⊤θ+εi and si=ti+u~i, where the pairs (u~i,εi) are independent and identically distributed, u~i and εi are independent with mean zero and finite variances, the first coordinate of u~i is zero (so that si keeps the constant and Σ~ has zero first row and column), and Cov(u~i)=Σ~. Then the least squares coefficient vector from regressing y on s converges in probability to 𝛉(A+Σ~)−1Aθ.

prp-eiv-nonidentified.title: The slope is identified only up to an interval
prp-eiv-nonidentified.title_html: The slope is identified only up to an interval
prp-eiv-nonidentified.html: Let (W,Y) be bivariate normal with covariance matrix entries σww,σwy,σyy, where σwwσyy>σwy2. If σwy≠0, a number b is the slope of some normal structural model with σx2>0, σu2≥0 and σ2≥0 that produces this distribution iff b lies in the closed interval with end points b1=σwyσww,b2=σyyσwy. If σwy=0, the only such slope is b=0.

prp-eiv-response.title: Error in the response
prp-eiv-response.html: Under these assumptions 𝛃Y∗=α+β⊤x+(ε+V), a linear model with the same coefficients and error variance σ2+σv2. If ε and V are normal, so is their sum, and all the exact theory of Parts II and III applies to Y∗ with σ2 replaced by σ2+σv2.

prp-eiv-simex.title: SIMEX in the linear model
prp-eiv-simex.html:
Assume the conditions of @thm-eiv-attenuation(c), with one mismeasured scalar regressor of error variance σu2, and fix ζ≥0. For each b, the naive least squares coefficients from the remeasured data converge with probability one to g(ζ)=(gx(ζ),gz(ζ)), where 𝛃𝛑gx(ζ)=βxσx⋅z2σx⋅z2+(1+ζ)σu2,gz(ζ)=βz+(1+ζ)σu2σx⋅z2+(1+ζ)σu2βxπ,{#eq-eiv-simex-limit}

and so does their average over b. Moreover:

  1. gx(−1)=βx and 𝛃gz(−1)=βz;

  2. every coefficient has the form a+b/(c+ζ) with c=1+σx⋅z2/σu2; in particular 1/gx(ζ) is linear in ζ when βx≠0;

  3. if a polynomial of fixed degree is fitted by least squares to the points 𝛉(ζk,θ^(ζk)) on a fixed grid, the SIMEX estimate converges to the value at −1 of the polynomial fitted in the same way to (ζk,g(ζk)), which in general differs from g(−1).

prp-eiv-tests.title: Which tests survive classical error
prp-eiv-tests.html:
Assume @eq-eiv-true-model and @def-eiv-classical with a single mismeasured scalar X, ε∼N(0,σ2) independent of (X,z), and the covariance matrix of (X,z⊤)⊤ positive definite. Consider the least squares regression of Y on (1,W,z).

  1. If βx=0, the usual t test of “the coefficient of W is zero” has exactly its nominal level.

  2. If βx≠0 and 𝛑π≠0, the usual F test of “the coefficients of z equal 𝛃βz” rejects with probability tending to one as n→∞.

prp-eiv-weak.title: The exact distribution with one instrument
prp-eiv-weak.title_html: The exact distribution with one instrument
prp-eiv-weak.html:
Let yi=βxi+ei and xi=πzi+vi, i=1,…,n, with fixed zi, Szz=∑izi2>0, and (ei,vi) independent bivariate normal with means zero, standard deviations σe,σv and correlation ρ, |ρ|<1. Let β^=∑iziyi/∑izixi and μ=πSzz/σv.

  1. β^−β has the same distribution as σeσv⋅ρη+1−ρ2ξμ+η,η,ξ∼iidN(0,1).{#eq-eiv-weak-representation}

  2. E|β^|=∞ for every μ.

  3. As μ→∞, (μσv/σe)(β^−β)→N(0,1) in distribution. If μ=0, β^−β has median ρσe/σv, which is the large-sample bias of least squares when π=0.

  4. (∑izixi)2/(σv2Szz)∼χ2(1,μ2), with mean 1+μ2.

thm-eiv-attenuation.title: Attenuation
thm-eiv-attenuation.html:
Let (x(i),z(i),u(i),εi), i=1,2,…, be independent copies of (x,z,u,ε) with finite second moments, satisfying @eq-eiv-true-model and @def-eiv-classical. Write t=(x⊤,z⊤)⊤ for the true regressors, s=(w⊤,z⊤)⊤ for the observed ones, 𝛉𝛃𝛃θ=(βx⊤,βz⊤)⊤, Σtt=Cov(t), assumed positive definite, and Σ~=diag(Σuu,0) for the covariance matrix of the error in s. Let α^n and 𝛉θ^n be the least squares intercept and slopes from regressing Y on s in the first n observations. Then, with probability one:

  1. 𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉θ^n→θw=(Σtt+Σ~)−1Σttθ=θ−(Σtt+Σ~)−1Σ~θ, and 𝛍𝛉𝛉α^n→α+μt⊤(θ−θw), where 𝛍μt=E(t);

  2. with a single regressor and no z, the slope converges to λβ;

  3. with a single mismeasured scalar X and exactly measured z, the coefficient of W converges to λx∣zβx and the coefficients of z converge to 𝛃𝛑βz+(1−λx∣z)βxπ, where 𝛑𝛔π=Σzz−1σzx is the vector of coefficients from the best linear prediction of X from z (@thm-rv-blp);

  4. the residual sum of squares divided by n (or by n minus the number of coefficients) converges to 𝛉𝛉σ2+θ⊤Σtt(Σtt+Σ~)−1Σ~θ, which in case (b) equals σ2+λβ2σu2.

thm-eiv-correction.html:

Assume that E(ε)=0, E(tε)=0, E(u~ε)=0, E(tu~⊤)=0, E(D)=Σ~=E(u~u~⊤), and that A=E(tt⊤) is positive definite. Let 𝛉A^n=1n∑i=1n(sisi⊤−Di),θ^mm=A^n−11n∑i=1nsiyi.{#eq-eiv-corrected}
